title: Hip Line vs Shoulder Line
shortDefinition: Hip line and shoulder line are the two rotation axes that decide passes, pins, escapes, and back exposure.
whyItMatters: You can clear the legs but still fail to pin if shoulder line remains free.
deepExplanation: Passing often begins with hip-line control, but pinning requires separating or locking shoulder line. Escapes reverse it: recover shoulder angle, then bring hip line back to guard.
beginnerView: Ask: can they still rotate shoulders or hips?
advancedView: Separate the two lines to create dilemmas: saving hips exposes shoulders, saving shoulders loses hips.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Hip Line vs Shoulder Line during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Hip Line vs Shoulder Line to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Hip Line vs Shoulder Line is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Hip Line vs Shoulder Line before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
